The strengths of a river flood include, in general, public attention, technological solutions, and disaster assistance. But many communities see only one or two of those three. Pick three towns on the prairie. Columbus, Nebraska has televisions groomed in low water pantsuits and podcasts and hazardous material cleanups and National Guard forces standing down. South Sioux City, 12 miles upstream, has an eight-thousand-dollar Claudia Schmidt, crooning Van Morrison, telling the water to take it back where it came from. And Hartington, 36 miles downstream, has houses wearing strapped boots and people who don't want to talk.

Where the Nebraska goes, print media tend to follow. A wire story comes out of Columbus with Ohio River crests and historic flood stagemarks and accusations about levee maintenance, but nothing from lower, quieter Hartington.

The floodplain below Gavins Point Dam has three nuclear power stations, a superfund site, and a hundred thousand people who generate their share of news each day. Its next blip above historical flood lines will be in Sioux City. The biggest communities served by its emergency spillway have stopped sending journalists down to look at them more than once. The superfund site could be as vulnerable to rising waters as anywhere else, but the structures are too solid to be worth minding.

Four regional online start-ups focus on the Cure Peace/Ash Grove/Missouri Basin/Platte River zone, but they languish. On a recent Sunday morning, their regional pages were fluff and opinion.

Five springs ago Paradise, Nebraska won a memorable case about the intentional release of flood waters in Missouri.

Two summers ago, Fremont, Nebraska hosted a plot of relict loess within which corn pushed its spring sprouts up through fisks of pavement.

A dedicated blogger covering rivers near Mullen, Nebraska has been collecting observations and sharing them with a tiny audience for almost two decades.

155. Café Cino

Sunday, April 30, 2000

I turn the Meuse Main on around midnight, try to talk myself out of the empty bottle of Amontillado in the carriage, the two bottles of vodka in the kitchen. I think maybe I could sleep with the windows open, try to sleep to the clank of loose window hinges. Commercial is doing loop-the-loops in the backyard, leaving puddles every other step. Outside the window the fountain burbles, and everybody who dares to hunt ghosts sits in their cars on battery-saving by the stairs, in slumped isolation. But seeing them reminds me I don't want to be alone.

The rain popped back up again. Maybe that's why I gave in and switched on the music. I'd heard that, out on the long gravel roads, it rained, actually rained like the sky was actually raining. Then I guess it was somebody's boyfriend-running late to Ibrahim's with flowers-who busted through the front doors dripping and dripping and looking positively disgusted at the "No Roma Terreur" placard. "This week only."

"Two years too late then."

The director bares his teeth. Wrong on so many levels. Baby-"Cat" looks apologetic, gentles him to the bar.

I rush for the kitchen. I need some whiskey. Maybe I can rinse out the vodka bottle and give it a fill, but maybe not. Maybe I'd better pour my one glass and get going before the rest of the pirates roll up close on their secret agenda. But on the way out, I forget something. I'm an idiot, andall the kitchen drawers are locked down with those heavy blue clips. I don't have a single thin instrument that'll force one.

At the other end of the building paved clouds are descending, a tide trying to scratch pebbles. Somebody tries to come in from the stairs and gets stalled in the doorway. Crackles, thinking. In language Italian surfers might understand. Palermo? Capri? Magic islands and salt spray? A thousand miles for a virgin world exactly the same as the old one.

I definitely need to go home.

The water was churning higher and faster by the minute. Curtis started filming it with his phone, but the camera just made snow lines of the tiny bubbles streaming in the beam of the headlights. Wes hauled himself awake as it reached the top board. The first line of watershed tally marks rode the crest up, spread forward, gurgled under, was followed by the next line, and new ones on the bank cut toward them. The tongue of water rushing in from the river grew fangs.

I ask Curtis to tell me what he got from the story, from all the reporting that went into it. Midway through the paper we'd pause to swim in a discussion of Joshua Berry, the lead writer. He didn't grow up in Southwest City and had only lived there for a year before the flood. He grew up in Texarkana and had spent two decades covering Deep South politics, policy, and economics at a trio of Arkansas newspapers. His parents had both died of a rare cancer when he was sixteen, and he got married during the same senior-year summer he wrote for the school newspaper and worked nights at a Texarkana Wal-Mart. Barely older than eighteen, he proposed to his girlfriend on graduation day, at her parents' house in the Ozarks, and left for Arkansas a few months later.

Southern journalists were more like sports reporters than professional assigners of meaning, Berry said. For local papers they followed a smaller scene without the luxury of context. Most left home before they were thirty, when everybody they knew was starting their lives.

When Berry was twenty-five he started running the state Bureau for the Texarkana Gazette, and on his third night on the job he walked into the newsroom just as the Gaylord-Ouachita fire department was dispatching twenty trucks. Two huge rigs had overturned on the freeway that ran past the station. UW-Madison was playing Texas on television in the lounge. It is common for a river to begin moving around, looking for places to escape its channel before it actually overflows. When this happens, the water is said to leave "bank-full." Bank-full can occur after hours or days of heavy rain, or during an all-day long winter ice shove, or even during a flash flood. The water in the channel may rise very gradually to the point where it begins to spill unobtrusively over the banks and flow away, or it may happen quickly, as when rain is falling in the watershed upstream at the same time the river is being restrained at a levee or dam downstream.

The booming city of 30,000 people was known as the Refining Capital of the World -- a nerve center for oil pipelines and railroads, miles of steel mills and factories. It was 60 miles north of Tulsa, Oklahoma, and had thrived since the 1880s, when the Missouri, Kansas, and Texas railroad came through.

Back on the river, Carver's Bend gained its name a few blocks to the south, when the Neosho turned sharply and exposed an oxbow between two loops, and then became known for steamboats that docked there. The town grew up around a squabbling woods full of oaks and pecans, and a steel mill that shipped products to Indianapolis and Detroit. Its people -- Prairie around the valley, Ozark up high, Cherokee baptized by their schools, and still more varieties of Baptist -- shopped at a brick corridor of main street that stretched just outside of downtown, where a redbone courthouse squeezed between striking Gothic spires and the red-brick, Romanesque post office with its martinsmoke and Doric column. They went to movies at the paling Art Deco Bijou, past the Hanger Museum and the parish library, and from the park, through the high-cast walled gate of the turreted Woodle mansion, all the way down to the town swimming pool with its lifeguards in iced tea and embroidered swim suits. They watched their pigskin champs from the stadium south of Nimrod Hill on Friday nights, and they flooded their grain elevator and telephone exchange every spring with regularity that might as well have been scheduled. In winter, if they drove south down county road 51, they could watch boys and girls bobsledding. Curtis bought two cups and sat watching the couple of TV sets. Curtis's cousin Pat brewed the coffee at the shop—they were high school classmates. The levee had held, Curtis told him, which seemed like some small good thing, or one of them anyway.

An older black man sat in a corner wearing a red work jacket, and held a halting conversation with Curtis and Pat. He told them he'd started working for the city concession at fairgrounds in 1972 and piloted his boat around the shower and toilet trucks. He remembered the floods of '84 and one from the late 80s or early 90s. As he spoke, he tapped a fist rough with liver spots against his leg, recounting his work, the food lines and soup kitchens, the safety trainings. Curtis had gone to him for help getting jobs around town, and the man's company had worked for the city. While the man spoke, Curtis thought about the combines and loaders the man had probably operated, the motels he would have built and cardboard he hauled. VESTA, Kan. – For the people of Anderson County, it was the worst night of a monumental week.

On March 13, Joplin, 100 miles to the southeast, would become America's storm-measuring unit, the EF-5 twister that flattened a third of its neighborhoods and killed 161 people – a seventh of its population. And for all the devastation in Joplin, Anderson's own brush with a December 2008 tornado – which left several people dead and homes leveled, all in the middle of a polar snowstorm – is seared into the minds of many Anderson residents as well.

For 24 hours beginning on that late winter night in 2011, townspeople and emergency officials on both sides of the Neosho sat frozen. They waited as the water crept higher.

They held their earth-moving equipment in reserve.

On both sides of the river, they hoped for the levee to withstand 25 feet of water.

And that is where the drama began in the late afternoon and stretching into the dark hours of March 13, 2011 in Anderson County. What happened that night that tested the resolve of a town and the skill and stamina of those who saved it. What happened that following Tuesday morning that crippled a community still picking up the pieces seven years later.

Preludes: The River Awakens

On March 12, a day before disaster would arrive in the middle of the night and turn this storied community into a national headline, most people in Anderson county were going about their days as they always did. Spring would begin coming to life next week and classes at the elementary school and at the junior college would resume within a few days, their winter breaks at an end.

At the back door of Madison Mitchell's country home outside Shoal Creek, the 28-year-old teacher was bathing nine-month-old junior, the little boy with the deep blue eyes who had learned to crawl and who already reminded his mother of herself.

Madison's husband Jonah was on his way to San Antonio that night, on his way to a Storycorps recording of a young man talking about moving on with his life after losing a parent to cancer.

"It was like my leg was met with concrete," Madison remembered. "I knew instantly that something was wrong."

The sky had opened up. Miles out, a wild storm was approaching.

When Curtis and Wes got back in the truck, he steered down the levee road and turned onto 67 toward town. They would listen for trouble on the radio, he told his son, and if the levee broke on the east side of the river, they'd head up the ridge north of town to the old VFW hall. He kept his gaze on 67's cracked and weedy shoulder as they reached the crest of the hill and the dashboard lights flickered over the fields beneath them.

Headlights moved in the distant darkness. As they came closer, Curtis saw a truck pull out in front of them, slow, and turn onto the county road that led across the floodplain and back toward the levee. A pickup loaded with furniture and piles of clothes. A couple in the cab and three in the back, all in pajamas. One of the men was talking on a cell phone, walking backward while he guided the truck. The truck's arrival lit something in Curtis that was already there, some fear he hadn't allowed himself to name. They passed, and the feeling stayed with him.

When they got to the crest of the hill, he turned left, back across the levee road and down the washboard driveway to the house, because this was home and it was too late to go anywhere else. He switched off the lights as they went in, so the house would look occupied even if it was empty. Someone outside shone a flashlight through the windows. Curtis watched from the living room as the beam swept back and forth over the furniture, the curtains. When it came around again, he waved.

"You'd better get off the island," he called, but the light had moved on. "Everybody needs to get off the island."

Flood-control engineers first began to build the steel-and-concrete levee system that protects Neosho, Missouri, from the final meanders of the Grand River in the 1940s. The formal association of levee districts to maintain them formed a few years later. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has maintained various sections since then, though the local districts are responsible for inspecting and maintaining the rest. When Neosho annexed the Pruitt Street neighborhood in 2005, its older homes became subject to the same codes as the rest of the town and were gradually brought up to the same standards of structural integrity as anyplace else. In 2006 a new berm was constructed behind the grain elevator and along the railroad tracks. In 2011 the levee was raised another eighteen inches.

People disagree about what's to blame for the failure one stormy April night two years ago. Some insist that paved streets in the expanding town sent more water into the river than the old fields did, and that a city now functions differently from a farm community when it comes to water running off buildings and pavement. Others point to increased runoff from the hills as more of the watershed has been cleared and subdivided, or to the diminished capacity of the river channel below Neosho to carry away the water the floodwaters dump.

Curtis had read about all of it. The sediment depended on which way the river was flowing. In a normal year it would deposit silt on the north bank and leave the rests of the old channel clean and dry. But this year the river might decide to cut through again. In which case, there was nothing the levee could do to stop it.

Scenes from Sinking Sands can be found on my writing blog, omitting the P. Allen Smith barge scene.
When I started out to write this scene for my new novel Sinking Sands (working title), I knew I wanted to show a person in Curtis Holland's position: a tenant farmer, living at the threshold between the levee-protected floodplain and the unprotected bottoms, downstream from a faulty levee on the edge of a small city. I wanted to convey the look and feel of such a place on the edge of a crisis, in a way that would show the texture of this world that's lost—it's not the New Orleans levees and the Industrial Canal, but in some ways it's much the same, a system we built to keep the river out, only to find it doesn't always work, and then what?

Curtis is a third-generation farmer. His family had gotten the farm in 1911, and like so many Midwestern farmers these days, he's struggling. curtains hollanntsinking sandsI wanted the setting and the stakes to both feel real to him and someone like him: not a matter of life and death as in a bigger disaster, but potentially ruinous and career- and legacy-ending. If the levee fails, his family's farm will be under feet of water and covered in silt; if it holds, the water will be diverted onto his land instead, possibly causing the same amount of damage.

The other thing I wanted to play with here was that moment when people in Curtis's situation can only refresh a webpage or check a phone app and watch the gauge ticking up, waiting for a confined catastrophe to unfold, powerless to do anything to stop it. The barge full of sandbags on its way upriver to plug a breech can make for a dramatic race-against-time set piece, but much of the drama of modern floodplain management is standing by watching a situation unfold, knowing that nature and human endeavors are both ultimately larger than any one person.

Curtis is also awaiting the worst possible news at his mill job: that the river has overtopped the levy and the pressure has caused a failure upstream. As it turns out, the levy behind the elevator holds, and the water comes over the land instead. Curtis will be at the mill at daybreak, the beginning of a long day of mud and work.

Curtis closed the Courier's website and closed his eyes. He imagined the water backing up against their field, climbing the gentle slope, rising inside the house. The photos of his father, leaning against the combine, would be gone. It had been a good life, a hard life, but a good life. Everything he'd ever known.

The seat beside him stirred. "Dad?" Wes mumbled, half awake. 

"You okay, son?" 

"What's happening?"

Curtis swallowed. "Just... watching the river." His voice sounded ragged.

"Will we lose it?" 

Curtis didn't answer. 

Suddenly, a tremor ran through the ground, through the pickup. Then another, and another. Wes sat up, eyes wide. 

"What was that?"

And then they heard it. A low, rumbling roar evolving into a grinding, shattering sound, like the earth was tearing itself open. The headlights swung towards the source, illuminating a dark, rising wave moving down the top of the levee. It wasn't water breaking *over* the levee. It was the levee *itself* collapsing.

Curtis instinctively threw his arm around Wes as the world exploded in a torrent of mud, water, and debris. The Courier's live feed went silent.

Curtis glanced at his son, then back at the oncoming water. The cost of sandbags for four hundred acres would be more than a year's worth of supplemental irrigation.

He saw a truck pull up on the county road, then drive slowly past. It was old man Miller, a retired farmer from up north. Miller slowed again, rolled down his window, and called out, "Curtis, you shouldn't be out here! You and Wes get to higher ground!"

"I'm just watching, Harold," Curtis shouted back, knowing the wind would carry his voice away. "Making sure everything's okay."

Miller squinted at him. "Everything ain't okay, Curtis. And you know it." He put the truck in gear and drove on towards town.

Curtis turned off the headlights. The field was dark, the river only a black shape pressing forward. He had to think about Wes. He could take Wes to his sister's in Kansas City. They could stay there as long as they needed to. 

But the farm. He looked at the house in the distance, the dark rectangle against the night. It wasn't just land and equipment and debt. It was generations. It was everything.

He still didn't know what he was hoping for, but he knew what he was fearing. He reached over and shook his son's shoulder.

"Wes," he said quietly. "Let's go."

"Where we going, Dad?"

"Just... somewhere safe." He didn't say the farm might not be.

As Curtis pulled out onto the county road, the Courier's live blog updated again:

12:47 a.m. BREAKING NEWS: The levee behind the grain elevator has breached. Water is now flowing rapidly into East Carver.

Curtis didn't stop the truck. He drove, but he didn't look back.

The levee held.

Curtis didn’t move. He sat there and watched the river cover his farm. He imagined what the next day would bring: the bloated cattle, the soaked corn stalks, the mud. He thought of all the work, the years of sweat and toil, washing away with the floodwater.

He knew what he had to do. He'd call the bank in the morning. He'd call his brother, he’d call Wes’s aunt.  He’d figure something out. He always had.

But right now, all he could do was sit there in the cold, listen to the thrum of the engine, and watch it all go under. He pulled his coat tighter around him. He just sat there, waiting for the dawn.

He drove on home a few minutes later. The house was dark and quiet. His wife, Mary, was asleep in their bedroom, and he knew she would be upset at him for waking her, but he needed to tell someone.

She sat up, pulling the quilt to her chest. "Curtis...no."

He didn't say anything. He couldn't.

"All those people..." she said softly. "The town..."

"I know," he said. 

Their silence stretched, broken only by the ticking of the grandfather clock in the hall.

"What about the farm?" Mary asked finally.

He looked at her. "I don't know."

Static.

“Tiber, this is Curtis Holland. You got a light on in the barn?”

More static. Then, a crackly voice, barely audible. "Holland? That you?"

“Yeah, Tiber, it’s me. Everything alright?”

“Well, son,” Tiber's voice was rough, full of age and something else. “Everything's about as alright as it can be, I reckon. I came down to check on things, and… well, Daisy’s sick.”

Daisy was Tiber's old, blind mare. Curtis had helped him doctor her a few times years ago.

“Sick how?”

“Colic. Bad. Been trying to get her to lie down all evening. I’m about wore out.”

Curtis looked out at the spreading water, at his farm being erased inch by inch. He glanced at Wes, sleeping soundly.

“Stay put, Tiber,” Curtis said. “I’m coming over.”

“Holland, you crazy? The water’s coming up!”

“I know, Tiber. That’s why I’m coming. Just hang on.”

Curtis put the truck in gear and turned off the county road, heading towards the river. The water was already creeping towards the gravel lane that led to Tiber’s place. He bumped along, accelerating when he could, praying he wouldn’t get stranded.

He found Tiber in the barn, kneeling by Daisy, stroking her nose. The mare was sweating and restless, letting out pained whinnies. The water was swirling around their ankles.

“Thought you weren't coming,” Tiber said, his voice edged with exhaustion.

“Had to try,” Curtis said, already reaching for the bottle of colic medicine he’d kept in his truck for years.
